name: DigitalOcean App Platform
tagline: Deploy a small containerized service with TLS, logs, and backups on one server

pricing.notes: Official Basic starting monthly container price.

tiers.name: Static Sites Free
tiers.limits: Up to 3 static-only apps; 1 GiB outbound transfer/app/month.

pricing.freeTierCaps: up to 3 static-only apps, each with 1 GiB outbound transfer/month
pricing.billingTerms: monthly usage billing; component compute is prorated per second with a 1-minute minimum; no annual plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: Extra static-only apps are $3/month; outbound overage is $0.02/GiB; development databases start at $7/month without backups; a dedicated egress-IP pair costs $25/app/month. Billing covers the first 28 days after component creation, and some rename/recreate operations can restart metering.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For DigitalOcean App Platform, deploy a small containerized service with TLS, logs, and backups on one server. The hard boundary is managed builds, runtime, scaling, databases, networking, and support, plus infrastructure scale, operations, and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Deploy a few trusted containerized services with TLS, route domains, retain logs, and perform backups on one user-owned server.
whatYouLose: managed builds, runtime, scaling, databases, networking, and support
ongoingBurden: patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for DigitalOcean App Platform because hosting products sell an operations team and failure-domain diversity, not merely a deploy button. The recurring cost buys patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Coolify
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosting platform for applications, databases, and services.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.desc: Deploy a container from Git, get TLS, logs, health checks, databases, and scheduled backups on your own server.

alternatives.name: Dokploy
alternatives.desc: A small self-hosted app platform with container deploys, TLS, logs, monitoring, and database backups.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Dokku
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Excellent at deploys and routing, but backups and a usable operations console are add-ons you assemble yourself.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Basic plan and a single-server personal platform DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for DigitalOcean App Platform in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Caddy, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a small Go control plane; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: deploy a few trusted containerized services with TLS, route domains, retain logs, and perform backups on one user-owned server.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Accept a Git repository or container image and one explicit Dockerfile-based build path.
Implement applications, environments, secrets, domains, health checks, and rolling container replacement.
Use Caddy for automatic TLS and route only to healthy local containers.
Capture bounded build and runtime logs and expose restart, rollback, and redeploy actions.
Back up PostgreSQL metadata and document backups for each deployed application's data volumes.
Add host metrics, disk alerts, update instructions, disaster recovery, and a prominent single-server warning.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-region or serverless infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out managed data stores and global edge delivery.
Deliberately leave out DDoS response, compliance, and guaranteed uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
